'''John M. Chowning''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|tʃ|aʊ|n|ɪ|ŋ}}; born August 22, 1934) is an American composer and acoustician. He is best known for developing a digital implementation of [[frequency modulation synthesis]].

==Technical innovations==
Chowning is known for having developed the frequency modulation (FM) synthesis algorithm in 1967.{{sfn|Johnstone|1994}}{{sfn|Schottstaedt|n.d.}}{{sfn|Chowning|1973}} In FM synthesis, one audio wave modulates the frequency of another, producing a resultant sound that can be periodic or non-periodic depending upon the ratio of their frequencies. He spent six years turning his breakthrough into a system of musical importance and eventually was able to simulate a large number of musical sounds. In 1974, [[Stanford University]] licensed the discovery to [[Yamaha Corporation|Yamaha]],{{sfn|Mattis|2001}} with whom Chowning worked in developing a family of synthesizers and organs. This was Stanford's most lucrative patent at one time.{{sfn|Pinch|Trocco|2004|loc={{Page needed|date=July 2020}}}}

The first commercial musical instrument to incorporate FM synthesis was the [[Synclavier]] I, introduced by [[New England Digital]] in 1977. Their Synclavier II, introduced in 1980, was frequently used in the production of popular music beginning that year. The first Yamaha product to incorporate the FM algorithm was the GS1, a digital synthesizer that first shipped in 1981. Yamaha introduced their first commercially successful FM synthesizer, the much less expensive [[Yamaha DX7|DX7]], in 1983. The DX7 was used on a host of popular songs throughout the 1980s, including [[Prince (musician)|Prince]]'s "[[When Doves Cry]]", [[A-ha]]'s "[[Take On Me]]", [[George Michael]]’s "[[Careless Whisper]]", and [[Sade (singer)|Sade]]’s "[[Smooth Operator]]". It has also been used extensively by composer [[Brian Eno]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Monroe |first=Jazz |date=2024-10-09 |title=John Chowning, godfather of digital pop: 'My wife told me: I didn't think I'd have to compete with a computer' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2024/oct/09/john-chowning-godfather-of-digital-pop-my-wife-told-me-i-didnt-think-id-have-to-compete-with-a-computer |access-date=2024-10-10 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

Another important aspect of Chowning's work is [[sound spatialization]].{{sfn|Chowning|1970}} Chowning developed an influential spatialization algorithm during the decade between 1962 and 1972. This period coincides with his initial years at Stanford University, first as a graduate student and later as assistant professor, an exceptional historical period during which he built a series of important collaborations with [[Leland Smith]], [[Max Mathews]], [[Manfred R. Schroeder]], [[Karlheinz Stockhausen]], David Poole, Andy Moorer, who all influenced his work.<ref>Zattra – Féron 2024b, pp.357–390.</ref><ref>Ibidem.</ref> In 1972, in his composition ''Turenas'', he was first able to create the illusion of a continuous 360-degree space using [[quadraphonic sound]].{{sfn|Mattis|2001}}

==Early life==
The first instrument Chowning learned was the violin, which he picked up after finding one in the attic of his family home; he then studied drums in high school. The [[Korean War]] had begun by the time he graduated, and instead of enlisting, Chowning auditioned for the [[United States Armed Forces School of Music|Navy School of Music]], which led to him performing in an 18-piece band on a Mediterranean aircraft carrier.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Monroe |first=Jazz |date=2024-10-09 |title=John Chowning, godfather of digital pop: 'My wife told me: I didn't think I'd have to compete with a computer' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2024/oct/09/john-chowning-godfather-of-digital-pop-my-wife-told-me-i-didnt-think-id-have-to-compete-with-a-computer |access-date=2024-10-10 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> After the war, Chowning graduated from [[Wittenberg University]] with a [[Bachelor of Music]] degree in 1959.{{sfn|Nelson|2015|loc=19}} He studied music composition with [[Nadia Boulanger]] in Paris from 1959 to 1961 before enrolling at Stanford, where he received his [[Doctor of Musical Arts]] degree in 1966, studying under [[Leland Smith]]. He was the founding director of the Center for Computer Research in Music and Acoustics ([[CCRMA]]) at Stanford, established in 1975.{{sfn|Mattis|2001}}

Chowning also worked for a number of years at [[IRCAM]] in Paris, and he and CCRMA were influential reference points in the founding of the French centre, with Chowning having repeated meetings and exchanges with [[Pierre Boulez]] in the 1970s.<ref>Féron – Zattra 2023, pp.123–132.</ref><ref>Féron – Zattra 2024a, pp.173–187.</ref>

==Compositions==
One of Chowning's most famous pieces is called ''[[Stria (composition)|Stria]]'' (1977). It was commissioned by IRCAM for the Institute's first major concert series called ''Perspectives of the 20th Century''. His composition was noted for its inharmonic sounds due to his famous FM algorithm and his use of the [[golden ratio|golden mean]] in music. With ''Phoné'' (1980–1981), he became the first to put FM over [[speech synthesis]].{{sfn|Anon.|2001}}

=== List of works ===
* ''Sabelithe'' (1966, revised 1971)
* ''Turenas'', (1972)
* ''Stria'' (1977)
* ''Phoné'' (1980–1981)
* ''Voices'' (2005)
